article_title: A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching
citation: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632
title: CDM-AIR: a capability–decision model ordering AI-TPACK upstream of TPB beliefs with context as antecedent and moderator
description: CDM-AIR is a theoretically grounded framework explaining teacher readiness to integrate AI in teaching. It separates capability from belief: AI-TPACK constitutes a capability system, while TPB constructs form a belief-mediated decision pathway. As the article states, "AI-TPACK constitutes a teacher’s capability system for designing and enacting AI-integrated pedagogy, whereas TPB constructs operate as a belief-mediated decision pathway through which teachers form intentions and translate them into observable classroom behaviour." Contextual facilitating conditions shape subjective norms and perceived behavioural control and moderate the PBC–behaviour link. The model is specified as thirteen hypotheses in five families and admits full structural, staged, and diagnostic modes of use.
requirements: Capability must be conceptualised as competence and measured with performance-based evidence where feasible, ordered upstream of decision beliefs
The teacher remains the accountable decision-maker; the model assumes AI functions through teacher-mediated adoption choices
constraints: The model does not model moment-to-moment distribution of agency between teacher and AI system during instruction
It has not yet been empirically validated; causal ordering remains theoretical until tested with longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs
Should classroom AI evolve to the point where systems adopt teachers rather than the reverse, the TPB decision core would require replacement rather than extension
target_learning_goals: readiness to integrate artificial intelligence in teaching
key_sources: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632

article_title: Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype
citation: McInnes, R., Airey, L., Moss, P., & Rathnappulige, S. (2026). Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 80–95. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11466
title: Critical discourse analysis framed by critical and post-digital literature as a lens on GenAI-in-pedagogy discourse
description: The article's analytical framework combines critical discourse analysis with critical and post-digital literature to interrogate how grey literature frames GenAI use in constructive alignment. The authors state they drew "on critical and post-digital literature to frame a critical discourse analysis" of grey literature on utilising GenAI in the constructive alignment process. The framework treats efficiency-promising discourse as an object of critique rather than a neutral account of practice.
requirements: A corpus of grey literature on GenAI in constructive alignment and a critical/post-digital theoretical framing
constraints: The analysis addresses grey-literature discourse in higher education; the article does not claim findings generalise beyond that discourse
target_learners: higher education educators, educational developers and policymakers
target_learning_goals: critical understanding of how GenAI discourse shapes pedagogical design practice
examples: The article interrogated grey literature on utilising GenAI in the constructive alignment process using a critical discourse analysis framed by critical and post-digital literature
key_sources: McInnes, R., Airey, L., Moss, P., & Rathnappulige, S. (2026). Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 80–95. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11466

article_title: A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation
citation: Jimmy de la Torre and Chia-Yi Chiu. (2016). A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation. Psychometrika, Volume 81, Issue 2, June 2016. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-015-9467-8
title: Cognitive diagnosis models posit multiple discrete skills, enabling finer-grained assessment than unidimensional IRT
description: The article frames CDMs against unidimensional item response models: unidimensional models "postulate a single underlying proficiency," whereas CDMs "posit multiple, discrete skills or attributes, thus allowing CDMs to provide a finer-grained assessment of examinees' test performance." The Q-matrix is described as a common CDM component for specifying the attributes required for each item.
requirements: A Q-matrix specifying the attributes required for each item
target_learning_goals: Fine-grained diagnosis of multiple skills or attributes
key_sources: Jimmy de la Torre and Chia-Yi Chiu. (2016). A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation. Psychometrika, Volume 81, Issue 2, June 2016. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-015-9467-8

article_title: Language learning, socioeconomic status, and child‐directed speech
citation: Schwab Jessica F., Lew-Williams Casey. (2016). Language learning, socioeconomic status, and child-directed speech. Wiley interdisciplinary reviews. Cognitive science. https://doi.org/10.1002/wcs.1393
title: Child-directed speech as a multi-feature input register whose prosodic, structural, and social characteristics differentially drive early language learning
description: The review organizes child-directed speech (CDS) as a speech register "characterized by higher pitch, shorter utterances, more repetition, and other features that differentiate it from adult-directed speech." It taxonomizes CDS features into sound-level (pitch contours, clarity), structural (isolated words, sentence frames, repetition), and social (contingency, referential transparency) characteristics, each linked to specific learning outcomes—phoneme discrimination, segmentation, word mapping, and grammar. The framework holds that features act differentially across learning domains and developmental windows, and that infants are active participants in eliciting CDS.
requirements: Caregiver input in naturalistic interaction; the framework concerns children learning language from caregiver speech rather than from screens or recorded media
constraints: The review notes few CDS-feature experiments have directly examined SES, and findings are drawn primarily from US samples
target_learners: infants and toddlers from birth through the third year of life
examples: Laboratory studies reviewed include segmentation of words from CDS but not ADS, faster noun interpretation in sentence frames, and word learning from repeated exposures across successive sentences
key_sources: Schwab Jessica F., Lew-Williams Casey. (2016). Language learning, socioeconomic status, and child-directed speech. Wiley interdisciplinary reviews. Cognitive science. https://doi.org/10.1002/wcs.1393

article_title: Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model
citation: Laura Brandl, Matthias Stadler, Constanze Richters, Anika Radkowitsch, Martin R. Fischer, Ralf Schmidmaier, Frank Fischer. (2024). Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09425-4
title: Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning (CDR) model relating individual characteristics, collaborative diagnostic activities, and diagnostic outcomes
description: The CDR model describes collaborative diagnostic reasoning in knowledge-rich domains by linking individual characteristics (content knowledge, collaboration knowledge, social skills) via collaborative diagnostic activities to diagnostic outcomes of accuracy, justification, and efficiency. It builds on the dual-search model of scientific discovery, treating evidence and hypothesis spaces as shared cognitive storages, and defines CDR as solving a complex problem collaboratively "by generating and evaluating evidence and hypotheses that can be shared with, elicited from, or negotiated among collaborators". This article tested the model empirically with a structural equation model across three simulation studies and proposed revisions.
requirements: Measurement of individual characteristics, CDAs, and diagnostic outcomes in a controlled simulation setting
constraints: Evidence so far comes from one domain, as the article notes that all studies were in the same medical domain, leaving cross-domain generalizability open
target_learning_goals: collaborative diagnostic reasoning skill in knowledge-rich problem-solving
examples: The simulation casts the learner as an internist collaborating with an agent-based radiologist to diagnose fictitious fever patient cases
key_sources: Laura Brandl, Matthias Stadler, Constanze Richters, Anika Radkowitsch, Martin R. Fischer, Ralf Schmidmaier, Frank Fischer. (2024). Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09425-4

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: Complex Dynamic Systems assumptions for an integrative motivation perspective
description: The article specifies CDS assumptions that allow motivational phenomena to be conceptualized as simultaneously individual and sociocultural: interdependence, irreducibility, and nonlinearity; dynamism, self-organization, emergence, and agency; attractor and repellor states; and control parameters, hierarchy, and self-similarity. The approach emerged "as an alternative to reductionist, deterministic, and linear cause-effect explanations, and which conceptualizes phenomena as holistic systems composed of interdependent, interacting elements." Agency is treated as a top-down process that co-acts with bottom-up self-organization, dissolving the dichotomy of automatic-unconscious versus agentic-conscious processes.
requirements: Research must identify the system's landscape of possible states and attend to behavior over time rather than averaging across diverse cases
constraints: The article cautions that because control parameters co-act interdependently, their influence cannot be understood by isolating or experimentally fixing them one at a time
Studies may foreground some system levels and background others while remaining cautious of conclusions of primacy
target_learners: All learners in culturally situated activity systems
target_learning_goals: Reconciling stability and change in motivation
examples: The article illustrates nonlinearity with a minor change in task difficulty triggering sudden total disengagement, while an intensive program might yield only minimal effect
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Refined CDST interpretation of emotions in SLA emphasizing temporal relationships among emotional factors over time
description: The article proposes a refinement of complex dynamic systems theory for second language acquisition in which emotions such as anxiety, enjoyment and boredom are conceptualized as trajectories that fluctuate across timescales, from seconds for word production to years for overall development. The authors state: "we emphasize the importance of examining the dynamic interplay among emotional factors over time, particularly the temporal relationship among factors." Unlike the current CDST framework, which focuses on longitudinal aggregate properties, this interpretation operationalizes both macro levels (development across conversations and classes) and micro levels (fluctuations within a single speech or sentence production), and treats temporal succession as a basis for inferring causality.
requirements: High-frequency time series data on emotions and language behaviours across timescales, since the framework requires observing how changes in one factor are followed by changes in another over time
constraints: The article notes that with the contemporary CDST understanding and traditional methodology, only a static relationship may be researched and demonstrated
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting emotional dynamics during second language learning and use
examples: The article presents a hypothetical graph (Fig. 2) in which an initial surge in enjoyment is followed by a fall in anxiety and later by an increase in boredom, illustrating potential temporal relationships among emotions concurrent with language behaviours
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: Complex dynamic systems (CDS) framing of student motivation: self-organizing, non-linear change, developmental cascades, and attractor states
description: The paper presents a primer on CDS as applied to motivation: psychological processes are organized systems embedded in layered environments; they are "self-organizing, adaptive, and emergent", change is non-linear, and small events can produce large change through developmental cascades. A central concept is that "there are certain patterns of psychological processing or behavior that students gravitate towards; these are called attractor states", which stabilize behavior but are hard to change; Heino et al.'s landscape metaphor represents them as valleys that interventions can deepen or flatten. The authors contend motivation is compatible with CDS because theories already posit socialization within nested systems, motivation shifts over time, and motivational forms are interconnected in emergent, reinforcing belief systems.
requirements: Interventions using this framing should consider how changes to classroom context (curricula, teacher practice) shift the attractor state landscape
constraints: The authors state it is beyond the article's scope to develop a complete integrated model of motivation based on this premise; empirical motivation research has largely used linear models
target_learning_goals: understanding and sustaining students' motivation, engagement, and learning
examples: The M-PLANS science motivation intervention used CDS as an underlying framework; Geerling et al. applied CDS to confusion and interest during a utility value intervention
key_sources: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w

article_title: Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue
citation: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3
title: 15-category classroom dialogue coding scheme revised from the Cambridge Dialogue Analysis Scheme with added silence codes
description: The study employed a coding scheme "revised from Cambridge Dialogue Analysis Scheme 52, with addition of codes for Structural Silence (SU) and Strategic Silence (SA)". It includes elaboration and reasoning invitations and responses, co-ordination invitation, simple and reasoned co-ordination, agreement, querying, reference back, reference to wider context, silences, and other codes, each with brief definitions and keywords in Table 1. The scheme captures features of exploratory and accountable talk such as building on ideas, justifying and challenging.
requirements: Interrater reliability assessment: kappa below 0.5 for a code required refinement and discussion between the two human coders, as done for RC, Q and OI
constraints: The scheme was revised considering the context of Chinese classrooms
target_learners: middle school students in mathematics and Chinese classes
target_learning_goals: categorising classroom dialogue turns to analyse productive talk
examples: Manual annotation by educational experts using this scheme served as the gold-standard benchmark against which GPT-4 coding was evaluated
key_sources: Long, Y., Luo, H. & Zhang, Y. (2024). Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue. npj Science of Learning 9:60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00273-3

article_title: The Effectiveness of Multimedia Application on Students Listening Comprehension
citation: Tagor Pangaribuan, Andromeda Sinaga & Kammer Tuahman Sipayung. (2017). The Effectiveness of Multimedia Application on Students Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p212
title: Researcher-designed CD-ROM multimedia application for listening comprehension
description: The article's multimedia application is "limited to the CD-ROM software which is designed by the researcher to help the lecturer in providing the listening materials". It replaces conventional tape-recorder delivery, in which lecturers had to replay dialogue manually and the sound was blurry. The application was evaluated by students across indicators such as material suitability, clarity of instructions, ease of understanding, navigation, music support, and interaction, receiving an overall mean quality score of 79.00 (Good).
requirements: Lecturers need the software to provide listening materials in place of manual tape-recorder replay
constraints: The article limits the multimedia application to CD-ROM software designed by the researcher
target_learners: sixth-semester students in listening comprehension classes at HKBP Nommensen University
examples: The experimental group was taught using the multimedia application while the control group was taught the conventional way without it
key_sources: Tagor Pangaribuan, Andromeda Sinaga & Kammer Tuahman Sipayung. (2017). The Effectiveness of Multimedia Application on Students Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p212

article_title: Effects of CDA Instruction on EFL Analytical Reading Practices
citation: Abduljalil Nasr Hazaea & Ali Abbas AlZubi. (2017). Effects of CDA Instruction on EFL Analytical Reading Practices. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(2), 88-101. https://novitasroyal.org
title: Fairclough-based three-level CDA framework for EFL analytical reading (description, interpretation, explanation)
description: The study develops a conceptual framework, based on Fairclough (1995) and Cots (2006), in which an EFL reading lesson is a communicative event and reading is a social practice. To reveal a discourse, students move through three levels: "text analysis (description), discourse analysis (interpretation) and critical discourse analysis (explanation)". Each level reveals one layer of meaning: text analysis describes lexicon, grammar and semantics; discourse analysis interprets text production, consumption and intertextuality; critical discourse analysis explains the writer's point of view and sociocultural background. The framework was operationalized as classroom stages and measured with a 39-item questionnaire and a validated test.
requirements: The three levels of analysis need to be operationalized in an EFL reading classroom, with teachers encouraging various interpretations instead of finding one point of view
constraints: The authors state results "are still general at the third level: the critical discourse analysis (explanation)"
examples: A class of 43 students used the framework for 14 weeks on textbook and newspaper texts
key_sources: Abduljalil Nasr Hazaea & Ali Abbas AlZubi. (2017). Effects of CDA Instruction on EFL Analytical Reading Practices. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(2), 88-101. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1171140

article_title: Effects of CDA Instruction on EFL Analytical Reading Practices
citation: Abduljalil Nasr Hazaea & Ali Abbas AlZubi. (2017). Effects of CDA Instruction on EFL Analytical Reading Practices. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(2), 88-101. https://novitasroyal.org
title: Three overlapping CDA analysis groups with integrated whole-class discussion
description: During treatment, students were divided into three groups, each addressing one stage of analysis, since the levels "can be simultaneously operationalized in an EFL reading classroom as three overlapping stages". Group A describes vocabulary and sentence structure using context; group B interprets by writing about the topic from background knowledge, putting students "in the position of writers rather than readers"; group C explains using a question list, bringing ideologies and reading against the text. Representatives then present results and an integrated analysis is discussed.
requirements: Teachers help groups extract meaning, encourage broader context use, and integrate the three layers in a whole-class discussion
constraints: The authors note that when using CDA's three levels, "not every CDA concept is equally useful"; facilitators and students can select tools
target_learning_goals: explanation of sociocultural dimensions of texts
examples: Group C students were encouraged "to resist the text; that is, to read against rather than with the text"
key_sources: Abduljalil Nasr Hazaea & Ali Abbas AlZubi. (2017). Effects of CDA Instruction on EFL Analytical Reading Practices. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(2), 88-101. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1171140

article_title: Effects of Agricultural Sales CDE Modules on Content Knowledge and Argumentation Skill
citation: Sapp, S. B., & Thoron, A. C. (2014). Effects of Agricultural Sales CDE Modules on Content Knowledge and Argumentation Skill. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(5), 93-110. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.05093
title: Agricultural sales training modules can develop content knowledge and argumentation skill without purposefully infusing argumentation
description: The study found that agricultural sales training modules, whether or not argumentation was infused, produced gains in content knowledge and argumentation skill among secondary agriculture students. The authors concluded that "argumentation does not need to be infused into agricultural sales training modules in order to see growth in content knowledge and argumentation skill," suggesting teachers can save planning time by not preparing to specifically teach argumentation.
requirements: Teachers implement the researcher-developed training modules aligned with the Agricultural Sales CDE over a preparation period of at least six weeks (21-24 hours).
constraints: The study was conducted over a six-week period, which the authors note may not have been long enough to see significant increases in argumentation skill.
examples: 37 students across nine schools completed modules with or without argumentation infusion; both groups gained on pretest-posttest measures.
key_sources: Sapp, S. B., & Thoron, A. C. (2014). Effects of Agricultural Sales CDE Modules on Content Knowledge and Argumentation Skill. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(5), 93-110. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.05093

article_title: Competency-driven hemostasis training reduces vascular complications in transradial hemodynamic monitoring: a self-controlled trial with early-career residents.
citation: Hou Qin, Zhou Bin, Kang Jing-Ping, Zuo Yun-Xia. (2025). Competency-driven hemostasis training reduces vascular complications in transradial hemodynamic monitoring: a self-controlled trial with early-career residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08048-z
title: Competency-Driven Hemostasis Training (CDHT): a three-component procedural skills training program
description: CDHT is a training program the authors developed for radial artery compression hemostasis, comprising "three progressive components": baseline assessment of residents' current techniques and outcomes, didactic instruction using a three-dimensional vascular reconstruction model plus evidence-based compression parameters, and supervised hands-on training with competency verification. In the study, 10 first-year anesthesiology residents completed it, and their patient outcomes before and after training were compared.
requirements: Baseline assessment of trainees' current techniques, didactic instruction, and supervised hands-on practice with competency verification, as the article structures the program
constraints: Evaluated only with anesthesiology residents at a single center; the authors state this may limit applicability to other specialties or settings
target_learning_goals: safe and effective radial artery compression hemostasis after catheter removal
examples: Ten first-year residents were assessed pre-training, received a 45-min didactic session with a 3D vascular reconstruction model, then completed supervised hands-on training with competency verification
key_sources: Hou Qin, Zhou Bin, Kang Jing-Ping, Zuo Yun-Xia. (2025). Competency-driven hemostasis training reduces vascular complications in transradial hemodynamic monitoring: a self-controlled trial with early-career residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08048-z

article_title: The application of the conceive-design-implement-operate combined with the problem-based-learning teaching method in an 8-year rotation system for obstetrics students in China.
citation: Chao Xiaopei, Li Xiaoyan. (2025). The application of the conceive-design-implement-operate combined with the problem-based-learning teaching method in an 8-year rotation system for obstetrics students in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07646-1
title: CDIO-PBL as complementary coupled educational strategies: CDIO contributes outcomes (goals) and PBL contributes processes (means)
description: The article presents CDIO-PBL as a combined teaching model in which the conceive-design-implement-operate framework, an engineering education model grounded in a "learning-by-doing" approach, is coupled with problem-based learning. The authors state that "the CDIO teaching model benefits from outcomes (goals) and the PBL teaching method benefits from processes (means)" and that the two are "overlapping and complementary in many aspects." In this study CDIO structured the hands-on skills cycle (conceive scenarios, design curriculum, implement via simulation, operate through end-of-cycle assessment) while PBL structured theoretical learning around real patient cases.
requirements: Requires instructors who can conceive clinical scenarios, design case-based curricula, run simulation-based implementation, and assess and refine each 2-week cycle
Requires access to real patient cases and simulation training models
constraints: The article notes no studies had previously reported this combined model in obstetrical education; evidence here is a single-institution pilot
examples: In the intervention group, teachers conceived clinical scenarios requiring hands-on procedures, designed a curriculum from existing patient cases, taught using simulation training models, and assessed and refined teaching at the end of each 2-week cycle
key_sources: Chao Xiaopei, Li Xiaoyan. (2025). The application of the conceive-design-implement-operate combined with the problem-based-learning teaching method in an 8-year rotation system for obstetrics students in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07646-1

article_title: Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda.
citation: Karoui Haykel, Rwandarwacu Victor P., Niyonzima Jonathan, Makuza Antoinette, Nkuranga John B., D'Acremont Valérie, Kulinkina Alexandra V. (2025). Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318284
title: Four-pattern taxonomy of irregular CDSA measurement data (skipper, mono-repeater, multi-repeater, wrongly evaluated) with three deviation levels
description: The article proposes a classification of irregular measurement-value patterns in CDSA log data used to detect clinical skill gaps. Signs per health center "were labeled with one of the four distinct pattern types (i.e., skipper, mono-repeater, multi-repeater, and wrongly evaluated)", each with a level of expression (mild, moderate, or severe) determined by how much statistical parameters (mean, IQR, missing-value frequency, value distribution) deviated from the combined average of all health centers. Skipper means high frequency of not-feasible/missing values; mono- and multi-repeater mean values concentrated around one or 2–3 values with small IQR; wrongly evaluated means high percentages of outlier or implausible values.
requirements: Numerical-valued clinical signs with informative distributions; a reference distribution (the article used the combined average of all health centers in the absence of a gold standard)
constraints: Does not apply uniformly to all signs (e.g., skipper does not apply to temperature, weight, and z-scores; wrongly evaluated does not apply to weight and height)
Deviation from the all-center average is a relative reference, not a gold standard
target_learners: healthcare workers in primary health centers
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and recording of clinical signs during consultations
examples: The taxonomy was applied to ten signs across 16 health centers (Table 3) to select the 10 lowest-performing centers for prospective observation
key_sources: Karoui Haykel, Rwandarwacu Victor P., Niyonzima Jonathan, Makuza Antoinette, Nkuranga John B., D'Acremont Valérie, Kulinkina Alexandra V. (2025). Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318284

article_title: A "flexible" compulsory dental basic research course for undergraduate students: a three-year retrospective study.
citation: Gan Xuejing, Ou Qianmin, Gong Zhuohong, Cai Gengbin, Liu Xinyu, Yang Ruihan, Lin Yuhang, Li Lin, Li Xiaolan, Hong Yun, Chen Zetao. (2024). A “flexible” compulsory dental basic research course for undergraduate students: a three-year retrospective study. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-024-04874-7
title: Hierarchical assessment system of the flexible CDBRC
description: A two-level assessment component of the CDBRC. At the basic level, "the course grades were comprehensively assessed by experimental course performance, literature review, and final exams, which can ease the academic burdens for students". The advanced level is optional and includes research projects, competitions, and research paper publications, allowing top-rated students to pursue deeper research engagement without raising the pass threshold for everyone.
requirements: Basic-level assessment must be comprehensive across experimental performance, literature review, and final exams so ordinary students can pass without advanced research output
constraints: The advanced assessment (projects, competitions, publications) is optional and depends on students voluntarily engaging beyond the compulsory core
target_learners: undergraduate dental students of varying ability levels
target_learning_goals: basic research skills and knowledge assessment
examples: The article reports the hierarchical assessment avoided causing obvious academic burdens while still training top-rated students through advanced research activities
key_sources: Gan Xuejing, Ou Qianmin, Gong Zhuohong, Cai Gengbin, Liu Xinyu, Yang Ruihan, Lin Yuhang, Li Lin, Li Xiaolan, Hong Yun, Chen Zetao. (2024). A “flexible” compulsory dental basic research course for undergraduate students: a three-year retrospective study. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-024-04874-7

article_title: Evaluation of a digital game for teaching behavioral aspects of clinical communication in dentistry.
citation: Lin Chia-Shu, Yang Cheng-Chieh. (2023). Evaluation of a digital game for teaching behavioral aspects of clinical communication in dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04040-7
title: CDPC game 'Dr. Doog, could you handle this for me?' — a 16-scene browser-based role-playing game for dentist-patient communication
description: The CDPC game is a web-browser digital role-playing game in which participants play a young dentist facing 16 scenes of challenging dentist-patient communication. "In most scenes, participants have two choices to decide how to interact with the patients, which leads to different results." A personified dog, Dr. Doog, acts as an advisor whose suggestions may be correct or misleading. Scenes were rated positively by five senior dentists/educators (average 4.7 on a five-point scale).
requirements: Playable via web browser on computer or mobile phone; completing all 16 scenarios takes less than 40 minutes
constraints: Scenarios are designed based on the clinical context of a local clinic in Taiwan and may differ from those in other countries
target_learning_goals: behavioral issues of clinical dentist-patient communication
managing patients with fear/anxiety or cognitive deficits
examples: Scene #1 depicts an elderly man with severe periodontitis demanding extraction of his loose front teeth
key_sources: Lin Chia-Shu, Yang Cheng-Chieh. (2023). Evaluation of a digital game for teaching behavioral aspects of clinical communication in dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04040-7

article_title: Learning to diagnose collaboratively: validating a simulation for medical students.
citation: Radkowitsch A, Fischer MR, Schmidmaier R, Fischer F. (2020). Learning to diagnose collaboratively: validating a simulation for medical students. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001344.shtml
title: CDR model of collaborative diagnostic reasoning with individual and collaborative activities
description: The CDR model describes collaborative diagnostic processes combining individual diagnostic activities (generating and evaluating evidence and hypotheses) with four collaborative activities: "sharing, elicitation, negotiation, and coordination". Evidences and hypotheses are kept in individual diagnostic spaces and become part of shared diagnostic spaces only when collaborators conduct these activities. The model underpins both the simulation design and the interpretation of validity results.
requirements: Collaborators must conduct the proposed collaborative activities for evidences and hypotheses to become part of a shared diagnostic space
constraints: The simulation operationalizes only one collaborative activity, information sharing, in a specific internist-radiologist context
examples: An internist diagnosing fever and shortness of breath consults a radiologist; the quality of shared information influences the radiologist's hypotheses and conclusions
key_sources: Radkowitsch A, Fischer MR, Schmidmaier R, Fischer F. (2020). Learning to diagnose collaboratively: validating a simulation for medical students. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001344.shtml

article_title: Opening the black box of selection.
citation: Sanne Schreurs, Kitty Cleutjens, Carlos F. Collares, Jennifer Cleland, Mirjam G. A. oude Egbrink. (2019). Opening the black box of selection. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09925-1
title: Cognitive Diagnostic Modeling (G-DINA) as a test theory for assessing the construct validity of selection procedures
description: The article applies G-DINA, a model in the family of cognitive diagnostic models, as a confirmatory test theory for selection data. It requires two inputs: a pre-specified Q-matrix (blueprint) and binary or ordinal applicant performance data. The article states it is "capable of dealing with multidimensionality between as well as within items", which Cronbach's alpha and the Omega coefficient cannot, because selection items each measure multiple competencies in varying combinations. The model tests whether the expected structure is found in the data and proposes alterations to the Q-matrix.
requirements: A pre-specified blueprint Q-matrix of intended competencies per item
Applicant performance data that are binary or ordinal
A sample size the article indicates must exceed a thousand test-takers for more specific models or ordinal analysis
constraints: The analysis does not search for additional constructs beyond those already in the blueprint
In this study the relatively small sample forced dichotomization of responses, so some richness of the data was lost
target_learning_goals: Assessment of interpersonal and cognitive competencies in selection procedures
examples: A saturated G-DINA model was applied separately to the V-SJT and WAT of the MUMS selection procedure, with Wald-based model selection per attribute
key_sources: Sanne Schreurs, Kitty Cleutjens, Carlos F. Collares, Jennifer Cleland, Mirjam G. A. oude Egbrink. (2019). Opening the black box of selection. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09925-1

article_title: Experimentos simples demostrando algunas propiedades de lentes difractivas y redes espirales
citation: José J. Lunazzi, Daniel S. F. Magalhães, Maria C. I. Amon, Noemi I. R. Rivera. (2008). Experimentos simples demostrando algunas propiedades de lentes difractivas y redes espirales. https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.0818
title: CD and DVD discs as classroom diffraction gratings for spectrometry demonstrations
description: Common digital discs serve as spiral diffraction gratings: the article reports that "Usualmente un CD tiene aproximadamente 650 líneas/mm y el DVD 1200 líneas/mm". Illuminating a disc with a small fluorescent lamp at 1-2 m and placing the eye a few centimetres away lets an observer see the lamp's discrete emission lines (Fig. 8, camera at z = 9,2±0,1 cm). The authors note "un elemento simple como un CD o DVD puede ser usado como ejemplo de espectrometría hasta en una sala de aula puesto que el experimento puede realizarse aunque haya luz ambiente". Transmission use is possible by removing the reflective layer.
requirements: A small-area or partially covered fluorescent lamp with discrete wavelengths at 1-2 m distance
For transmission geometry, a transparent CD from a 50-unit box or removal of the reflective layer by cutting the edge
constraints: The coloured spectra appear mainly with lamps that are not very extensive; the observation distance of a few centimetres places the eye on the white segment of the diffraction pattern where the validity condition of the model holds
target_learning_goals: introducing spectrometry with discrete emission lines
examples: A photograph taken with a camera at z = 9,2±0,1 cm from the disc shows the lamp's spectral colours, demonstrating the effect works with ambient light in a classroom
key_sources: José J. Lunazzi, Daniel S. F. Magalhães, Maria C. I. Amon, Noemi I. R. Rivera. (2008). Experimentos simples demostrando algunas propiedades de lentes difractivas y redes espirales. https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.0818
